evidence_items.summary: MaizeHorizon is a per-plant maize detection dataset recorded from a forward-facing RGB camera on a ground robot driving along crop rows towards the horizon. This viewpoint makes detection a far-field small-object problem: plants recede until they occupy a handful of pixels and merge into soil and canopy clutter. The record accompanies the paper Sensor pixels or network input: measuring the per-plant maize detection limit , and supports its central measurement: detectability is bounded by the lower of the detail the imaging chain delivers and the resolution the network input retains, and which of the two binds is measurable rather than assumed. First campaign (Dan Phuong, Hanoi, April 2025) 5,979 RGB frames at 1920x1080 across 28 forward-motion clips, recorded with a Logitech C920 in two maize fields over three days. Hand-labelled test set : 3 held-out clips, 120 frames, 4,067 plant instances and 941 ignore regions, stratified by pixels-on-target into near (2,747), mid (1,238) and far (82) tiers. An explicit ignore class covering the unresolved vegetation band near the horizon, so that far-field evaluation neither penalises correct detections nor rewards misses. Clip-disjoint splits for two training arms, preventing temporal leakage between near and far views of the same plant. Optically minted labels : 3,636 far-tier pseudo-label files and 10,355 near/far pairs of the same physical plant, obtained by detecting each plant when near and tracking it backward with optical flow. Metadata : human-verified per-plant count ledgers and the test-set box-area cumulative distribution. Second campaign (Nam Sach, Hai Phong, July 2026) 150 hand-labelled frames at 7680x4320 from a Samsung Galaxy S23, over two sessions, with 29,297 plant instances and 6,482 ignore regions (far tier 5,790 at input 1280, of which 2,324 below 12 px pixels-on-target). Recorded fifteen months later and about 70 km away, with the same mount, camera height and annotation protocol.
evidence_items.title: MaizeHorizon: a forward-motion, range-stratified per-plant maize detection dataset

evidence_items.summary: We report a multi-month engineering program to build Sophea, a production bilingual Greek-English automatic speech recognition system. We evaluate the system against nine production gates covering Greek and English word error rate, language identification, and hallucinations on non-speech audio. Across twenty-three training iterations and two model architectures, no training-data composition passed all nine gates simultaneously. Meeting the Greek noisy-environment target required about 1,500 steps of dense domain exposure, while preserving English language identification tolerated only about 250 steps, or about 1,250 with a rebalanced mix that reduced Greek accuracy. We describe a six-stage data pipeline in which calibrating an audio-quality filter against in-domain anchors reduced the discarded share of scored Greek audio from 98.7 percent to 10.6 percent. A pre-registered ablation isolated a hallucination defect to one training-data package. A three-model ROVER ensemble increased gate coverage from 4-7 of 9 for individual models to 9 of 9 and reduced overlapping-speech WER from 53.35 percent to 37.87 percent, a 29 percent relative improvement. A separate learned per-clip arbiter over two models is listed as sophea/asr-k1 (preview) on the public Open ASR Leaderboard, with 4.26 percent average WER across eight public English test sets, and reaches 25.88 percent WER on live Greek noisy-environment traffic. We also document five cases in which a measurement tool produced a plausible but incorrect result and seven substantial approaches that were evaluated but not shipped. No model weights or training data are released; we report methodology and quantitative results only.
evidence_items.title: Building a Production Greek-English Speech Recognizer

evidence_items.summary: Mixing services on Ethereum aim to break the links between source and destination addresses on-chain. As blockchain technology supports diverse ecosystems spanning decentralized finance (DeFi), supply chain systems, and Internet of Things (IoT) payment networks, mixing services are increasingly exploited to launder illicit funds across these domains. Address linking is therefore essential for anti-money laundering (AML) investigations and forensic analysis. Although existing methods attempt to address this issue, there are still two critical limitations: 1) insufficient and imprecise neighbor information utilization and 2) limited dataset representativeness and lack of practical evaluation methodology. Motivated by these limitations, we propose MixTracker, a graph-based framework for address linking in Ethereum mixing services. First, we construct an ego-subgraph for each address that comprehensively aggregates relevant transactions, providing sufficient neighbor coverage. Second, we encode ego-subgraphs with a dynamic graph attention encoder to adaptively weight informative neighbors, then apply a pairwise prediction head to produce accurate subgraph-to-subgraph link predictions. Third, we augment training data with supplementary data from addresses with informative labels identified through address reuse patterns. We also introduce a ranking evaluation methodology with case studies for practical validation. Experimental results show that our proposed MixTracker outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving $F1$ -score improvements of 0.035, 0.078, and 0.024 on three benchmark mixing datasets. In particular, on case study data from security incidents, MixTracker achieves 0.944 recall for classification and 0.833 Hit@10 for ranked retrieval within 365 days when trained with supplementary data, suggesting its potential for real-world investigations.
evidence_items.title: MixTracker: A Graph-Based Framework for Address Linking in Ethereum Mixing Services With Blockchain Security Applications

evidence_items.summary: Benchmark researchers and developers of large language models (LLMs) and other AI systems need to find relevant evaluations, locate their benchmark datasets and code, and understand the settings behind reported scores. We present Benchmark Radar, a living database and search engine for retrieval and discovery of AI benchmarks, covering LLM evaluation, agentic and tool-use benchmarks, coding, reasoning, safety, and domain-specific evaluations. The system combines daily discovery of benchmark papers, repositories, datasets, and releases with a searchable benchmark catalog, mentions in model cards and technical reports, and score histories. It retains source identities and citations so readers can inspect candidate benchmarks and their evaluation evidence. Daily discovery draws on 37 sources: 13 direct connectors and 24 first-party research and engineering feeds. The catalog contains 1,283 source records drawn from 4 benchmark catalogs and 12,916 numeric observations on 790 records. We describe collection and retrieval, audit the full catalog, and examine benchmark saturation, adoption trends, and the limits of score comparisons. A worked example walks through a complete prior-art search, showing how to query the catalog and inspect benchmark evidence when designing a new evaluation. We release the web dashboard with a benchmark leaderboard, a Pareto frontier view of score against measured use, saturation and trend views, daily feeds, downloadable evidence, a command-line interface (CLI) for offline queries, and reproducible analysis.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark Radar: A Living Database and Search Engine for AI Benchmarks and Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background. Measured performance of thyroid ultrasound artificial intelligence depends on both cohort characteristics and the evaluation endpoint. We assessed frozen models across public cohorts with differing label provenance, separating evaluation against malignancy outcomes from agreement with ultrasound risk categories. Methods. Five backbones were trained on 387 thyroid ultrasound images from 385 public cases (222 papillary thyroid carcinoma, 163 benign) labelled by postoperative diagnosis; 1,332 fine-needle aspiration cytology blocks from the same archive formed a separate benchmark. Exact and perceptual near-duplicates were grouped before image-level partitioning; per-image patient identifiers were unavailable, so patient-level independence could not be confirmed. Frozen models were evaluated on a TN3K subset (n = 1,228; dataset-provided benign/malignant labels) and for concordance with an endpoint derived from radiologist Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (TI-RADS) categories in DDTI (n = 637), without retraining or threshold adjustment. Results. On TN3K the ensemble reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.825 (95% confidence interval 0.800–0.849) and ResNet-50 reached 0.888 (0.870–0.904). Against the TI-RADS-derived endpoint, AUROC was 0.477 and 0.437, indicating little agreement with that categorisation. Because cohort, acquisition and endpoint changed together, this contrast cannot be attributed to label definition alone. The cytology benchmark reached AUROC 0.986 (0.970–0.998) against 0.733 for the ultrasound ensemble, a descriptive non-paired contrast. Conclusions. Frozen models performed differently across cohorts differing in acquisition and outcome definition. The findings support explicit reporting of label provenance, cautious interpretation of cross-cohort contrasts, and patient-level external evaluation against a clinically appropriate reference standard.
evidence_items.title: Cross-cohort evaluation of thyroid ultrasound deep learning across different outcome definitions: a duplicate-controlled benchmark

evidence_items.summary: From the perspective of the current development trend of large language models, full evaluation on complete test sets entails high computational, time, and financial costs and cannot meet the need for frequent and rapid testing. Anchor-point evaluation relies on a small number of representative anchor samples to approximately assess the overall performance of a model, making it a feasible solution for low-cost and efficient evaluation. However, this method depends heavily on the quality of the anchor samples and the design of the evaluation framework, and it has evident shortcomings in terms of data distribution shift, sample noise, experimental conditions, and error control. This paper summarizes various problems in anchor-point evaluation from the two levels of datasets and model evaluation, compares optimization approaches such as active sampling, domain adaptation, data denoising, weighted evaluation, and multidimensional robust evaluation, and discusses the scope of application and constraints of general optimization solutions. Active sampling and lightweight data correction can improve the stability and accuracy of anchor-sample evaluation; in contrast, complex domain adaptation, multilevel adversarial experiments, and large-scale error analysis have excessively high computational costs, weakening the core lightweight advantage of anchor-point evaluation. Future research needs to balance evaluation accuracy, computational efficiency, and actual business needs, with an emphasis on developing lightweight and reliable anchor-point evaluation solutions suited to few-sample scenarios.
evidence_items.title: Research and Analysis of Dataset and Model Evaluation Limitations and Optimization Solutions Based on the Anchor-Point Evaluation Method
